overview: Founded by Phoenician settlers on the Gulf of Tunis, Carthage became the centre of a powerful Punic network linking North Africa, western Mediterranean islands and Iberia. Ports, inscriptions and archaeological remains show a place of traders, craftspeople and families as well as generals. The map uses “Carthaginian Empire” and “Carthage” for successive slices of this same history; the later Roman city on the site was a different political phase.

periods.title: Phoenician settlement and a growing port
periods.summary: UNESCO dates Carthage’s foundation to the ninth century BCE. Its legendary founder Dido belongs to later stories; the settlement and its maritime connections are historical. The map’s first Carthaginian label begins much later, around 500 BCE.

periods.title: A western Mediterranean power
periods.summary: From the sixth century BCE Carthage developed a wide commercial and political reach. Its ports and links to western islands mattered, while civic offices and councils governed at home. A map polygon cannot show every local alliance or changing degree of control.

periods.title: War over Sicily
periods.summary: Rome and Carthage fought their first major war from 264 to 241 BCE. Carthaginian coins issued in Sicily helped pay armies; their tiny Punic words can tell us something a battle map cannot: officials had to organize money.

periods.title: Hannibal and a second war
periods.summary: Carthage remained a major power after the first war. Hannibal marched across the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE, but the second war ended in a Roman victory in 201 BCE.

periods.title: A city under pressure
periods.summary: Carthage remained inhabited and active after Hannibal’s defeat. A third war began in 149 BCE. Rome captured and destroyed the Punic capital in 146 BCE; the imported map’s end dates of 200 or 100 BCE do not give this historical endpoint.

periods.title: The site after Punic rule
periods.summary: A Roman Carthage later rose over the Punic city’s ruins. Its theatre, baths and other later remains belong to that Roman phase, not automatically to Punic builders. Punic people and traditions beyond the destroyed capital did not all vanish in 146 BCE.

items.text: The archaeological site preserves Punic harbour remains. They anchor Carthage’s maritime story in physical infrastructure, although the surviving basins cannot by themselves tell us the cargo or crew of every voyage. Ships and ports connected communities around the western Mediterranean.

A British Museum gallery describes silver coins that Carthage minted in Sicily between about 400 and 300 BCE to pay armies. Some carry short Punic inscriptions meaning “in the land,” “of the paymaster” or “in the camp.” Even an army needed accountants; these coins are evidence of organized payments, not of what every sailor or soldier earned.

Carthage was governed through elected chief officials often called suffetes or shofetim, councils and public assemblies. Our picture comes mainly from later Greek and Roman writing, checked against inscriptions, so the precise powers and who could participate are debated. It was a city with institutions, not simply Hannibal giving orders to everyone.

The Louvre’s Punic stelae and an Ohio State edition of a Carthaginian temple tariff also preserve names of dedicators and rules for offerings. They show people making vows and priests administering a sanctuary. Those records are narrow windows into religious life; they do not tell us what every family believed.

sections.title: A house with water close at hand

items.text: At Kerkuane, a separate Punic town on Cape Bon, excavators found houses entered through corridors into courtyards. Some plans included wells, washbasins and baths, with rooms arranged around the open centre. That gives a concrete glimpse of domestic space in Carthage’s wider Punic world; it is not a floor plan of every Carthaginian home.

Kerkuane also preserves streets, shops and workshops. Its visible ruins mostly belong to the late fourth and early third centuries BCE; the town was abandoned around the middle of the third century and not built over by a Roman city. That is why these ordinary workspaces survive more clearly than much of Punic Carthage.

Excavations at Bir Massouda in Carthage found two structures interpreted as household latrines and a third as a public latrine. Their construction dates to about the late fifth or early fourth century BCE. The evidence is unusually specific: archaeology can reveal where people dealt with the least glamorous part of city life.

Those three latrines help researchers study waste collection, but they do not prove every home had a toilet or that Carthage had modern plumbing. If you are wondering whether ancient history includes toilet questions: the archaeologists were wondering too.

sections.title: A small clue to caring for children

items.text: A spouted Punic pottery vessel from Carthage, dated to the first half of the third century BCE, is catalogued as a feeding bottle. Its shape offers a rare object connected with caring for young children. The object does not reveal who held it, what was inside, or how common such vessels were.

A limestone stela catalogued by the Louvre as AO 5175 begins with the Punic words 𐤋𐤓𐤁𐤕 𐤋𐤕𐤍𐤕 (LRBT LTNT): “to the Lady, to Tanit.” This is a modern Unicode rendering of the attested consonant letters, not a photograph of the carving. Punic is the language; the Phoenician-derived alphabet is its script. The stone records a dedication, not the literacy of every Carthaginian.

The same stela names Baal Hammon and its dedicator, with his father and grandfather. The Louvre says its final words are not yet understood. A family name on a stone can outlast an empire, but historians must still leave unread words unread.

sections.title: An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book

items.text: A surviving Carthaginian inscription, known as KAI 74, sets out what priests received from different offerings. One clause exempts a worshipper poor in livestock from a priestly share. It is a rule on a stone, not proof that every sanctuary followed it in every century.

Roman writers admired an agricultural work associated with the Carthaginian Mago. Later Greek and Latin versions carried its farming advice, including guidance on trees, into Roman literature. The Punic original does not survive intact, and modern scholars debate whether “Mago” was a single author or a name attached to collected knowledge.

Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps in 218 BCE was a startling military feat, but it did not win the second war. Roman victory in 201 weakened Carthage; the city still existed for more than fifty years before the third war and the siege that ended in 146 BCE.

In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Punic capital and enslaved its surviving inhabitants. The Roman city built later on the site is part of Carthage’s long history, but its monuments are not evidence that Punic Carthage possessed Roman theatres or baths. People and Punic cultural practices elsewhere in North Africa continued through political change.

ending.text: Rome captured and destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE, ending it as an independent capital. Survivors faced enslavement, while a Roman city later rose on the same ground. The political power ended; this was not the extinction of everyone with a Punic language or tradition. The map’s two imported labels and rounded years describe coverage, not two different Carthaginian civilizations or a historical end in 100 BCE.
